Ashikaga shogunate: Japan. The Ashikaga clan governed Japan from the Imperial capital of Heian-kyō (Kyoto) as de facto military rulers along with the daimyō lords of the samurai class.

Siege of Sarajevo: Bosnia and Herzegovina. The city was initially besieged by the Yugoslav People's Army, before they were replaced by elements of the newly-formed Army of Republika Srpska.
In which country was Tokugawa shogunate?
Tokugawa shogunate: Japan. The Tokugawa shogunate, also known as the Edo shogunate, was the military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868.

Kingdom of Prussia: German Empire. The Kingdom of Prussia (German: Königreich Preußen, pronounced [ˈkøːnɪkʁaɪç ˈpʁɔʏsn̩]) was a German state that existed from 1701 to 1918.

Achaemenid Empire: Medo-Persia. At peak, its territorial extent was roughly 5.5 million square kilometres (2.1 million square miles), making it the largest empire of its time.

Red Terror: Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic. Volodarsky in alleged retaliation for Bolshevik mass repressions, the Red Terror was modeled on the Reign of Terror of the French Revolution, and the Paris Commune.

Abbie Hoffman (November 30, 1936 - April 12, 1989) was an American political and social activist who co-founded the Youth International Party ("Yippies") and was a member of the Chicago Seven.

This Indian politician served three non-consecutive terms as Chief Minister of Rajasthan — starting in 1998, 2008, and 2018 — after earlier representing Jodhpur in the national parliament. Who is he?

Ashok Gehlot (born 3 May 1951) is an Indian politician who served as the Chief Minister of Rajasthan from 1998 to December 2003, then again from 2008 to December 2013, and later from 2018 to December 2023.

Sparked by riots in Brussels after a nationalist opera performance in August 1830, this uprising split the mostly Catholic southern provinces from the Dutch-led union to form a new kingdom — which event?

Belgian Revolution was a conflict which led to the secession of the southern provinces (mainly the former Southern Netherlands) from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and the establishment of an independent Kingdom of Belgium.
Installed as high priest by the Roman procurator Valerius Gratus, this New Testament figure is described as the organizer behind Jesus's trial before the Sanhedrin — who was he?
Caiaphas was a High Priest of Israel during the first century.

This monarch's court physician, Johann Friedrich Struensee, effectively ran Denmark and Norway for two years before being overthrown in an 1772 coup, after which the ruler's own son eventually acted as unofficial regent — who was he?
Christian VII (29 January 1749 - 13 March 1808) was King of Denmark and Norway and Duke of Schleswig and Holstein from 1766 until his death in 1808.
After 37 years in the U.S. Army commanding forces in Iraq and Afghanistan, this four-star general traded the uniform for the spy chief's chair before resigning in 2012 — who is he?

David Petraeus (born 7 November 1952) is a retired United States Army general who served as the fourth director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) from September 2011 until his resignation in November 2012.
Son of a chambermaid and a carpenter, this British politician led the Conservatives, served as PM from 1970 to 1974, and was also a keen yachtsman and musician — who is he?
Edward Heath (9 July 1916 - 17 July 2005) was a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1970 to 1974 and Leader of the Conservative Party from 1965 to 1975.
On 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese forces under General Van Tien Dung captured South Vietnam's capital, triggering a frantic evacuation and ending the Vietnam War — what is this event called?

Fall of Saigon was captured by North Vietnam on 30 April 1975. The aftermath ushered in a transition period under the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam until the formal reunification in 1976.
Described by Homer as the most handsome of mortals, this Trojan youth was abducted by the gods to become Zeus's cup-bearer on Olympus — who is he?
Ganymede (mythology) (Ancient) is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy.

The first Democrat elected president after the Civil War, this former Buffalo mayor and New York governor holds a unique distinction: he's the only president to serve two nonconsecutive terms. Who was he?
Grover Cleveland (March 18, 1837 - June 24, 1908) was the 22nd and 24th president of the United States, serving from 1885 to 1889 and from 1893 to 1897.
A Jewish refugee who fled Nazi Germany in 1938, which Harvard-trained diplomat later served as national security advisor and secretary of state under Nixon and Ford?
Henry Kissinger (May 27, 1923 - November 29, 2023) was an American diplomat, political scientist, and politician.

This nomadic people swept out of Central Asia into Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE, pushing Goths and Alans westward and building a vast but short-lived empire on Rome's Danube frontier — who were they?

Huns were a nomadic people who lived in Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE. By 370 CE, the Huns had arrived on the Volga, causing the westwards movement of Goths and Alans.
Sailing from Brittany, this explorer charted the Saint Lawrence River and gave a nation its name using the Iroquoian term for the villages at Stadacona and Hochelaga — who is he?
Jacques Cartier (31 December 1491 - 1 September 1557) was a French maritime explorer from Brittany.
Appointed by George W. Bush as ambassador to the United Nations, this attorney and diplomat later returned to government as a national security advisor in 2018 — who is he?
John Bolton (born November 20, 1948) is an American attorney, diplomat, Republican consultant, and political commentator.
This Polish statesman became the country's first Marshal and is regarded as the father of a republic re-established in 1918, 123 years after Poland had last been partitioned — who is he?
Józef Piłsudski (5 December 1867 - 12 May 1935) was a Polish statesman who served as the Chief of State (1918-1922) and first Marshal of Poland (from 1920).
This Soviet politician led the USSR for just over a year, from February 1984 until his death in March 1985, capping a career that began in Komsomol propaganda work. Who is he?
Konstantin Chernenko was Leader of the Soviet Union from 1984 to 1985.

This 16th-century struggle for a Baltic territory saw Russia's early gains at Narva and Dorpat eventually checked by an alliance of Sweden, Denmark-Norway, and Poland-Lithuania — what's this conflict known as?
Livonian War (1558-1583) concerned the control of Old Livonia (in the territory of present-day Estonia and Latvia).
Working as a nurse in New York's slums, this campaigner for legal contraception helped develop the first birth control pill and founded a major reproductive-health organization — who is she?
Margaret Sanger (ne Higgins; September 14, 1879 - September 6, 1966) was an American birth control activist, sex educator, writer, and nurse.
Called 'the defining event of modern' this country's history, it raged from 1910 to 1920 and put revolutionary generals in power for the next two decades — what was it?
Mexican Revolution was an extended sequence of armed regional conflicts in Mexico from 20 November 1910 to 1 December 1920.
This Hebrew prophet led his enslaved people out of Egypt and, according to scripture, received a divine law that became part of the Torah — who is he?
Moses was the Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of slavery in the Exodus from Egypt.
This Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin appears only in the Gospel of John, where he's drawn to Jesus's teachings and, some traditions hold, becomes a secret disciple — who is he?
Nicodemus is a New Testament figure venerated as a saint in a number of Christian traditions.

A Waffen-SS commando who helped rescue Benito Mussolini in the daring Gran Sasso raid, this operative later led Operation Greif, infiltrating German soldiers behind Allied lines in enemy uniforms, and was acquitted at a 1947 war-crimes tribunal — who is he?
Otto Skorzeny (12 June 1908 - 5 July 1975) was an Austrian-born German in the Waffen-SS during World War II.

Ruhollah Khomeini (17 May 1900 - 3 June 1989) was an Iranian politician and Shia cleric who served as the first supreme leader of Iran from 1979 until his death in 1989.
Fluent in Sinhala and Dhivehi from his early diplomatic postings in Sri Lanka, this Russian official has served as foreign minister since 2004, longer than anyone since the Soviet era — who is he?
Sergey Lavrov (born 21 March 1950) is a Russian diplomat who has served as Minister of Foreign Affairs since 2004.

Stefanos Kasselakis (born 29 March 1988) is a Greek businessman, entrepreneur and politician who previously served as the leader of Syriza.

This de facto independent East Asian state emerged after the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, drew rival British and Russian interest, and lost its independence to the People's Republic of China in 1951 — which state?
Tibet (1912–1951) was a de facto independent state in East Asia that lasted from the collapse of the Qing dynasty in 1912 until its annexation by the People's Republic of China in 1951.
This Indian Army captain was posthumously awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest military honor, after being killed fighting at Point 4875 during the 1999 Kargil War — who is he?
Vikram Batra (9 September 1974 - 7 July 1999) was an Indian Army officer.

William McKinley (January 29, 1843 - September 14, 1901) was the 25th president of the United States, serving from 1897 until his assassination in 1901.

Álvaro Arzú (14 March 1946 - 27 April 2018) was a Guatemalan politician and businessman who served as the 44th president of Guatemala from 1996 to 2000, as well as several terms as Mayor of Guatemala City.
Prime Minister during the years Turkey joined NATO and fought in Korea, he became the last Turkish leader executed after a military coup, hanged in 1961 — who was he?

Assassination of Kim Jong-nam: 2017 murder in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

Battle of Agincourt: 1415 English victory in the Hundred Years' War. The Battle of Agincourt ( AJ-in-kor(t); French: Azincourt [azɛ̃kuʁ]) was an English victory in the Hundred Years' War.

Bhima: Second Pandava in the epic Mahabharata. Bhima's life was filled with extraordinary episodes that showcased his strength and bravery.

Burning Man: Annual experimental event in Nevada, US.

Centrism: Political alignment in the middle of the left–right political spectrum.

Croatian War of Independence: 1991–95 war during the Yugoslav Wars.

A physician turned journalist, this French prime minister demanded total victory after 1.4 million of his countrymen died in the First World War and pushed through the Treaty of Versailles's harsh terms. Who was he?
Georges Clemenceau: Prime Minister of France (1906–1909, 1917–1920)

Catherine the Great's favourite, lover, and possibly her secret consort, this Russian statesman died mid-negotiation over a treaty ending a war with the Ottomans that he himself had overseen — who was he?
Grigory Potemkin: Russian military leader and statesman (1739–1791)
After his mother's second marriage to Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, this German industrialist later co-ran his father's empire, holding a stake in BMW and battery maker VARTA — who is he?

This Byzantine emperor's early reign saw the Persians overrun Syria and Egypt after a defeat at Antioch, yet he rebuilt his army and drove them all the way back, winning a decisive victory in 627 — who is he?

Sparked on 10 May by a sepoy mutiny in Meerut and finally crushed at Gwalior in June 1858, this uprising challenged British East India Company rule — what is it called?

Indian Rebellion of 1857: Uprising against British Company rule. The rebellion began on 10 May 1857 as a mutiny of sepoys of the company's garrison in Meerut, a town 40 miles (64 km) northeast of Delhi.

Jack Kemp: American politician and football player (1935–2009)
Born in Shawinigan Falls, Quebec, this Liberal first entered the Commons in 1963 and served under Pearson and Trudeau before becoming Canada's 20th prime minister in 1993 — who is he?
Jean Chrétien: Prime Minister of Canada from 1993 to 2003.

Elected monarch of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1674, this military commander first made his name fighting in the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge before achieving fame against the Ottomans — who was he?
John III Sobieski: Ruler of Poland–Lithuania from 1674 to 1696.
One of the Twelve Apostles, this figure betrayed Jesus to the Sanhedrin for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in the Garden of Gethsemane — who is he?
Judas Iscariot: Disciple and betrayer of Jesus.
Impeached by the Texas House in 2023 by a vote of 121–23 after securities-fraud charges dating back to 2015, this Republican has served as Texas attorney general since 2015 — who is he?
Ken Paxton: American politician and lawyer (born 1962)
This horned Alpine folklore figure accompanies Saint Nicholas each December, swatting badly behaved children with birch rods while good kids get small gifts — who is he?
Krampus: Christmas figure in Alpine folklore. In this tradition, Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with small gifts, while Krampus punishes badly behaved ones with birch rods.
Belgians nicknamed him the "Builder King" for his lavish public works, but he was also the sole private owner of the Congo Free State — which monarch, who reigned 44 years, was he?
Leopold II of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1865 to 1909.
Married to Marie Antoinette in 1770, he was the last man to be styled King of France before the monarchy fell during the Revolution — who was he?
Louis XVI: King of France from 1774 to 1792.
Dying sometime after 1326, this woman was the second wife of Osman I, founder of the Ottoman dynasty, and the mother of his successor — who was she?
Malhun Hatun: Wife of Osman I.

A young French aristocrat who volunteered for Washington's Continental Army, he commanded troops at the decisive siege of Yorktown and is still celebrated as a hero in both France and the United States — who was he?
Marquis de Lafayette: French military officer and politician (1757–1834)
In the Hebrew Bible, this king of Salem and priest brought out bread and wine to bless Abraham after a great battle — who is he?
Compiled in the late second or early third century CE, this text is the first written record of Judaism's Oral Torah and underlies both the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds — what is it called?
Mishnah: First major written collection of the Oral Torah.
Serving as Saudi Arabia's intelligence chief from 2005 to 2012, this prince was briefly crown prince for just three months in 2015 during his half-brother's early reign — who is he?
Muqrin bin Abdulaziz: Saudi royal, military official and former Crown Prince (born 1945)
Declared emperor by the Senate at nearly 66 after Domitian's assassination, this former servant of Nero who helped expose the Pisonian conspiracy ruled Rome only from AD 96 to 98 — who was he?
Nerva: Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98. Nerva (born Marcus Cocceius Nerva; 8 November 30 – 27 January 98) was a Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98.
Killed at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 and canonized a year later, this 'Eternal King of Norway' became a saint whose veneration helped spread Christianity among the Vikings — who was he?
Olaf Haraldsson: King of Norway from 1015 to 1028.

This 19th-century South American conflict was the deadliest interstate struggle in Latin American history, pitting one nation against an allied trio of neighboring countries from 1864 to 1870 — which conflict?
Paraguayan War: Major international war in South America (1864–1870)

The younger brother of Louis XIV and founder of a cadet branch of the House of Bourbon, this 17th-century French royal, known simply as 'Monsieur,' won a notable military victory over William of Orange at the Battle of Cassel. Who was he?
Philippe I, Duke of Orléans: French prince (1640–1701)
Zeus punished Prometheus for giving fire to humanity by chaining him to a rock where an eagle ate what, every day?
The liver regrew each night so the punishment could repeat forever -- the Greeks had noticed that the liver, alone among organs, regenerates.
An Abrahamic faith born in 1930s Jamaica, it has no central authority and centers on Jah — with many followers regarding Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as the Second Coming. What is it?
Rastafari: Abrahamic new religious movement originating in 1930s Jamaica.

This American fantasy author sold more than 90 million copies of his 14-book epic saga, having earlier in his career written tie-in novels featuring a sword-and-sorcery barbarian created by another writer. Who is he?
This politician resigned as Kyrgyzstan's acting president in November 2020 just so he could run in — and win — the 2021 election that made him the country's sixth president. Who is he?
Sadyr Japarov: President of Kyrgyzstan since 2021. Japarov returned to Kyrgyzstan in 2017, where he was arrested and sentenced to an 11 year prison term due to his prior illegal political activities.

Depicted in reliefs at Ramesses III's mortuary temple, this mysterious maritime confederation was long blamed for Late Bronze Age raids on Egypt around 1200 BC, though scholars now see them more as a symptom of the era's collapse than its cause. Who were they?
Sea Peoples: Purported ancient tribal confederation of the Late Bronze Age.
Serving five separate terms as prime minister between 1995 and 2022, this long-time Nepali Congress leader saw his tenure dogged by accusations of nepotism and corruption — who is he?
This left-wing ideology is defined by social ownership of the means of production — public, cooperative, or employee-held — rather than private ownership. What is it?
Socialism: Political philosophy emphasising social ownership of production.
Nicknamed the 'Tiger King' for his ferocity, this 29th monarch of the Ayutthaya Kingdom is credited with devising the fundamental techniques of Muay Thai — who is he?

Thai Sa: King of Ayutthaya. The name "Thai Sa" (lit. "behind the pool") refers to the Banyongrattanat Palace, which was located by a pool where he often resided.
Author of the Port Huron Statement and one of the 'Chicago Seven' defendants, this 1960s New Left activist later served in the California legislature and was once married to Jane Fonda — who is he?

Highly regarded as a military strategist, this Vietnamese general led communist forces to victory across the decades-long Indochina wars, while also serving as minister of defense and deputy prime minister. Who is he?
Võ Nguyên Giáp: Vietnamese general and communist politician (1911–2013)

One of three brothers with distinguished military careers, this British general rose to Commander-in-Chief, America, during the War of Independence after famously scaling the cliffs at Quebec in 1759. Who was he?
William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe: British Army officer and politician (1729–1814)

Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Robert Boyle is a physicist. Robert Boyle (25 January 1627 – 31 December 1691) was an Anglo-Irish natural philosopher, chemist, physicist, alchemist and inventor.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Otto Hahn is a chemist. Otto Hahn (German: [ˈɔtoː ˈhaːn]; 8 March 1879 – 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
What is the atomic number of Einsteinium?
Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
In what year was Jean Tatlock born?
Jean Tatlock: Jean Frances Tatlock (February 21, 1914 – January 4, 1944) was an American psychiatrist.
In what year did Nikola Tesla die?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
In what year was Chlorine discovered?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
Mikoyan MiG-35: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Marketed as a 4++ generation jet fighter, it is a further development of the MiG-29M/M2 and MiG-29K/KUB fighters.
In which country is Fish and chips?
Fish and chips: United Kingdom. Fish and chips is a hot dish consisting of battered and fried fish, served with chips.
Who is credited with discovering Rhodium?
Rhodium: William Hyde Wollaston. Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
Who is credited with discovering Ibuprofen?
Ibuprofen: Stewart Adams. Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
Who is credited with discovering Carbon?
Carbon: Antoine Lavoisier. Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Drugs that meddle with this neurotransmitter can do everything from paralyze to cause convulsions, since it's the signal motor neurons use to activate muscles. What is it?
Acetylcholine (ACh) is an organic compound that functions in the brain and body of many types of animals (including humans) as a neurotransmitter.
With one stable isotope and the rank of 12th-most-abundant element in the universe, this lightweight metal carries atomic number 13 — what is it?
Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13.
It can't touch a virus or a fungus, but a few varieties even fight protozoa — this class of drug is the frontline weapon against bacterial infection; what is it?
Antibiotic is a type of antimicrobial substance active against bacteria.

Driven mainly by elevated LDL cholesterol, this chronic inflammatory disease quietly builds plaque-filled lesions in artery walls until, often by middle age, it can trigger a stroke or heart trouble — what is it?
Atherosclerosis is a pattern of the disease arteriosclerosis, characterized by development of abnormalities called lesions in walls of arteries.
Usually the tenth-brightest star in the night sky, this red supergiant in the constellation Orion varies noticeably in brightness over a roughly 400-day cycle — name the star?
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star in the equatorial constellation of Orion. Its Bayer designation is α Orionis, Latinised to Alpha Orionis and abbreviated Alpha Ori or α Ori.
Despite being fully Turing-complete, this minimalist 1993 esoteric language allows only eight commands and takes its unusual name from a slang term for utter confusion — what language is it?
Brainfuck is an esoteric programming language created in 1993 by Swiss student Urban Mller.
This biological family includes domestic dogs, wolves, coyotes, foxes, and jackals, found on every continent except Antarctica. What family is it?
Canidae (from Latin, canis, "dog") is a biological family of caniform carnivorans, constituting a clade.
Which American political scientist drew fierce controversy as co-author of the 1994 book 'The Bell Curve' and author of the welfare-system critique 'Losing Ground'?
Charles Murray (political scientist) (born January 8, 1943) is an American political scientist.
Its glorious blue in glass and paint was long wrongly blamed on bismuth, and frustrated miners named its ore after a goblin. Which hard, gray element carries the symbol Co?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Tolerant of poor, sandy soil, this legume was domesticated in Africa millennia ago and is now grown far more in Nigeria and Niger than anywhere else on Earth — which crop?
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
When insulin runs short, the body burns fat into acidic ketones, causing deep gasping breaths and fruity-smelling breath in this potentially life-threatening emergency — what is it?
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a potentially life-threatening acute complication of diabetes mellitus.
Trained in both mathematics and philosophy, which Austrian-German thinker developed the concept of phenomenological reduction and founded a major 20th-century school of philosophy?
Edmund Husserl (Austrian; 8 April 1859 - 27 April 1938) was an Austrian-German philosopher and mathematician who established the school of phenomenology.
This class of chemical compounds forms when the hydrogen of an acid's hydroxyl group is replaced by a carbon-based group, and includes the fatty-acid derivatives called glycerides. What is it?
Ester is a compound derived from an acid (either organic or inorganic) in which the hydrogen atom (H) of at least one acidic hydroxyl group (OH) of that acid is replaced by an organyl group (R).

With over 2,400 described species, these soft-bodied beetles produce light mainly at twilight, an ability that likely began as a larval warning signal before evolving into an adult mating display. Name this insect family?
Firefly are a family of elateroid beetles with more than 2,400 described species, many of which are light-emitting.
Its name comes from Greek words meaning "study of the earth," and this science examines the rocks and processes that shape not just our planet but other astronomical bodies too — what field is it?
Geology is a branch of natural science concerned with the Earth and other astronomical bodies, the rocks of which they are composed, and the processes by which they change over time.

This German physicist turned his eye on the mind itself, founding psychophysics and giving his name to a law showing that sensation rises with the logarithm — not the raw intensity — of a stimulus. Whose pioneering work was it?
Gustav Fechner (19 April 1801 - 18 November 1887) was a German physicist, philosopher, and experimental psychologist.
Sometimes called urticaria, this itchy rash of raised welts can flare for minutes or days, may follow an allergy or infection, and in half of all cases has no identifiable cause — what is it?
Hives is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh-colored, raised, itchy bumps.
First used ritually by forager tribes in Central Africa and later adopted by Gabon's Bwiti tradition, this psychoactive plant alkaloid interacts with both opioid and serotonin receptors — what is it?
Ibogaine is a psychoactive indole alkaloid derived from plants such as Tabernanthe iboga, characterized by hallucinogenic and oneirogenic effects.
The first woman ever to chair the Federal Reserve, she later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — a Brooklyn-born, Yale-trained economist. Who is she?
Janet Yellen (born August 13, 1946) is an American economist who served as the 78th United States secretary of the treasury from 2021 to 2025 and as chair of the Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2018.
Born in 1972, this Canadian atmospheric scientist holds an endowed public-policy chair at Texas Tech and in 2021 became Chief Scientist at the Nature Conservancy — who is she?
Katharine Hayhoe (born 1972) is a Canadian atmospheric scientist.
This Swiss polymath founded the study of graph theory and topology, and introduced much of modern mathematical notation, including the concept of a function — who is he?
Leonhard Euler (15 April 1707 - 18 September 1783) was a Swiss polymath who was active as a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, logician, geographer, music theorist and engineer.
Named for their strong, monogamous pair bonding and the long stretches paired birds spend sitting together, this small genus of African parrots is popular as a pet — what is it commonly called?
Lovebird is the common name for the genus Agapornis, a small group of parrots in the Old World parrot family Psittaculidae.
Covering everything from B2B deals to a government's 'Got Milk?'-style campaigns, this business pillar means acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers — what is this discipline called?
Marketing is the act of acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers. It is one of the primary components of business management and commerce.
This Hungarian-American psychologist identified and named the highly focused, creativity-boosting mental state known as 'flow' — who is he?
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (29 September 1934 - 20 October 2021) was a Hungarian-American psychologist.
Caused by antibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, this autoimmune disease most often weakens the muscles of the eyes, face and throat — which disease?
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a long-term neuromuscular junction disease that leads to varying degrees of skeletal muscle weakness.
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American thinker is considered the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines. Who was he?
Norbert Wiener (November 26, 1894 - March 18, 1964) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and philosopher.
Often linked to polycystic ovary syndrome or pelvic inflammatory disease, this fluid-filled sac can cause severe pain if it ruptures or twists — what is it?
Ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac within the ovary. If the cyst either breaks open or causes twisting of the ovary, it may cause severe pain.
This aromatic herb is a natural hybrid between watermint and spearmint, native to Europe and the Middle East but now cultivated worldwide — what plant is it?
Peppermint (Mentha piperita) is a hybrid species of mint, a cross between watermint and spearmint.
This GABA-derived drug treats cognitive disorders, vertigo, and dyslexia, and shares its 'racetam' drug class with related compounds like levetiracetam and aniracetam — what is it?
Piracetam is a drug that has efficacy in cognitive disorders, vertigo, cortical myoclonus, dyslexia, and sickle cell anemia; sources differ on its usefulness for dementia.

This mammal genus includes a familiar, masked, ring-tailed nocturnal visitor common across North America, plus two lesser-known tropical relatives; its closest kin are the ring-tailed cats and cacomistles. What animal is this?
Procyon (genus) is a genus of nocturnal mammals comprising three species commonly known as raccoons in the family Procyonidae.
A medium-sized tropical tree native to Southeast Asia, it's a close relative of the lychee and longan and shares its name with the edible fruit it bears — what is it?
Rambutan (Nephelium lappaceum) is a medium-sized tropical tree in the family Sapindaceae.
Native to West Africa and later naturalized across Asia and the West Indies, this plant's stems yield fibre while its calyces are steeped for a popular infusion — what is it?
Roselle (plant) (Sabdariffa gossypiifolia) is a species of flowering plant in the genus Sabdariffa that is native to Africa, most likely West Africa.
First described in 1779, which large African raptor stands over four feet tall on stilt-like legs and is grouped in its own family, Sagittariidae?
Secretarybird (Sagittarius serpentarius) is a large bird of prey that is endemic to Africa.
With symbol Na from the Neo-Latin 'natrium' and a single stable isotope, this reactive metal sits in group 1 and is found in minerals like halite and feldspar — what is it?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.

This medical emergency occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or reduced, causing cell death — its warning signs include facial drooping and sudden difficulty speaking or moving one side of the body. Name the condition?

Stroke is a medical condition in which blood flow to a part of the brain is reduced or blocked causing cell death. There are two main types of stroke: ischemic, due to lack of blood flow, and hemorrhagic, due to bleeding.
Caused by Clostridium tetani, this infection brings on recurring muscle spasms that can last weeks and prove fatal in about 10% of cases — what is it commonly known as?
Tetanus (from Ancient Greek 'tension', 'stretched', 'rigid'), also known as lockjaw, is a bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani and characterized by muscle spasms.
When water loss to the air outpaces uptake by the roots, plants shut tiny leaf pores to conserve moisture, slowing this evaporative water-movement process — what's it called?
Transpiration is the process of water movement through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts, such as leaves, stems and flowers.
Native only to the wetlands of the Carolinas, which carnivorous plant snaps shut a 'jaw' formed from the tips of its leaves when an insect trips it?
Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States.
Common across Europe and also found in Asia, this large carpenter bee bores its nest into dead wood rather than building a hive — which species?
Xylocopa violacea is the common European species of carpenter bee, and one of the largest bees in Europe.
Taken by mouth, smeared as a cream, or injected, this antiviral medication is a frontline treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles. What is it?
Aciclovir: Antiviral medication used against herpes, chickenpox, and shingles.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, it clears out an alarming roll call of intestinal parasites — pinworm, hookworm, ascariasis, giardiasis and more. Which medication is it?
Commonly called buffalo, this large grazing mammal endemic to North America is one of just two living species in its genus, alongside a European cousin — what animal is it?
American bison: Species of bovid artiodactyl mammal.

Characterized by extreme food restriction and a fear of gaining weight despite being underweight, this eating disorder is described in the DSM-5 as involving a disturbance in how one perceives their own body shape — what's the condition called?
Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder. Individuals with anorexia nervosa have a fear of gaining weight, despite the fact that they are typically underweight.
Sold under the brand name Abilify, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and irritability linked to autism spectrum disorder — what is it?
Aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazole is taken by mouth or via injection into a muscle.
Evolving from a troubled twin-engine predecessor into a four-engine heavy bomber powered by Rolls-Royce Merlin engines, which British WWII aircraft became one of the RAF's most famous bombers?
Avro Lancaster: World War II British heavy bomber aircraft.
This common, noncancerous enlargement of a male gland can cause frequent urination and a weak stream; it isn't linked to poor hygiene, and there's no known cure. What's the condition?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.
Your blood type is set by antigens sitting on the surface of which cells?
Inherited proteins, carbohydrates and glycolipids on the red cell surface define the group. Some of the same antigens appear on other tissues too.
Grown on one of the Amazon's largest and longest-lived trees, this selenium-rich edible seed comes in a shell weighing up to 2 kilograms combined with its fruit. What is it?
Brazil nut: Species of tree and its edible seeds.
Native to tropical Africa, this gourd-producing vine yields fruit that can be eaten young as a vegetable or dried and hollowed out into bowls, ladles, or even musical instruments — what is it?
Calabash: Species of bottle gourd plant.
Ranked the world's richest person by Forbes from 2010 to 2013, this Mexican tycoon built his fortune largely through telecommunications and remains Latin America's wealthiest individual — who is he?
Around 20 millimetres long with a shimmering structural-green shell and a coppery underside, this beetle is identified by its isosceles-triangle scutellum — which species?
Cetonia aurata: Species of beetle. The scutellum is the small V-shaped area between the wing cases; it may show several small, irregular, white lines and marks.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.
Home to crows, ravens, magpies, and jays, this bird family boasts a brain-to-body ratio rivaling great apes, and one of its members even passed the mirror self-recognition test — what family is this?

A Scottish biologist, classicist and mathematician who pioneered theoretical biology, he's remembered for his 1917 book On Growth and Form, which opened the way to explaining how patterns and body structures take shape — who was he?
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson: Scottish biologist, mathematician, and classics scholar.
Defined as having at least three loose or watery bowel movements in a single day, this condition is most often caused by an intestinal infection from contaminated food or water — what is it?

Diarrhea: Loose or liquid bowel movements. Diarrhea (American English), also spelled diarrhoea (British English), is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day.
Element 105 sparked a long Cold War naming dispute, claimed first by a Soviet institute in 1968 and then by Berkeley in 1970 before being settled in 1993 — which synthetic element?
Dubnium: Chemical element with atomic number 105 (Db)
The second-largest member of the deer family, this animal is also called "wapiti," a Shawnee and Cree word meaning "white rump" for the pale fur it flashes to signal alarm — what animal is it?
Elk: Species of deer. The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose, Alces alces, but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.

In 2019 this French-American MIT economist shared the Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for an experimental approach to fighting global poverty, rooted in the randomized trials of her J-PAL lab — who is she?
This front-of-the-head body part houses most sense organs — eyes, nose, and mouth — and its damage or scarring can profoundly affect a person's sense of identity. What is it?
Face: Front of a head. The face is the front of the head in humans and many other animals that features most of the sense organs including the eyes, nose and mouth.
This normal, occasionally embarrassing bodily process brings intestinal gas to the rectum, pressurizes it with muscle contractions, and releases it through the anus — what is it?
Flatulence: Bodily function of expelling intestinal gas from the anus.

After dropping out of Harvard to help build early versions of Windows at Microsoft, this developer co-founded a studio that made Half-Life and later launched a digital storefront called Steam — who is he?
Known only from teeth and four jawbones, this extinct genus of giant ape roamed China for nearly two million years and is now thought to be a close relative of the orangutan — what is it?
Gigantopithecus: Extinct genus of primate. The species may have been sexually dimorphic, with males much bigger than females.
One of the heaviest snakes alive, which non-venomous constrictor prefers shallow, slow-moving South American waters like flooded grasslands and rivers?

Nicknamed the 'Halloween beetle' in North America for invading homes each October to overwinter, this extremely color-variable insect was introduced there from eastern Asia to control aphids — what species is it?
Harmonia axyridis: Species of beetle. Harmonia axyridis is a lady beetle or ladybird species that is most commonly known as the harlequin, Asian, or multicoloured Asian lady beetle.
The offspring of a stallion and a female donkey, this equine hybrid is the rarer reciprocal cross to the mule and was often mistaken in European folklore for a horse-cow hybrid — what is it?
Hinny: Domestic horse–donkey hybrid. It is the reciprocal cross to the more common mule, which is the product of a male donkey (a jack) and a female horse (a mare).
First made in Belgium in 1956 and sold under the brand names Atarax and Vistaril, this first-generation antihistamine also treats anxiety and insomnia — what drug?
Hydroxyzine: Antihistamine drug. It is used in the treatment of itchiness, anxiety, insomnia, and nausea (including that due to motion sickness).
This probability principle holds that a randomly typing creature, given endless time, would almost surely reproduce the complete works of Shakespeare — what's it called?
Infinite monkey theorem: Counterintuitive result in probability.
This neo-Keynesian economist gave his name to a model for censored data — the 'tobit' — while advising the Fed and championing government action against recessions; who is he?
James Tobin: American economist and Nobel Laureate (1918–2002)
This French mathematician ranged across number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics — and a crater on the Moon is named after him; who was he?
Endemic to a handful of Indonesian islands, this apex predator is the largest living lizard — males reaching 3 metres and 150 kg — and hunts in groups, a rarity among reptiles. What is it?
Komodo dragon: Largest living species of lizard. The largest extant population lives within the Komodo National Park in Eastern Indonesia.
Together with pikas, this mammal family — comprising rabbits and hares — makes up the order Lagomorpha and includes over 70 species — which family?
Leporidae: Family of lagomorphs. Leporidae is the family of rabbits and hares (Lepus), containing over 70 species of extant mammals in all.
Nicknamed the 'Dragon Lady,' this single-engine American spy plane flew covert missions above 70,000 feet over the Soviet Union, China, and Cuba from the 1950s — what is it?
First named in 1703 to honor a French botanist, this genus of 200-plus flowering trees and shrubs produces large fragrant blooms and cone-like autumn fruits — which genus?
Magnolia: Genus of angiosperms. Magnolia is a large genus of about 210 to 340 flowering plant species in the subfamily Magnolioideae of the family Magnoliaceae.
Awarded the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta, this German physicist originated quantum theory and lent his name to a fundamental physical constant — who is he?
Sold under the brand name Robaxin and developed in 1956, this centrally acting muscle relaxant treats short-term musculoskeletal pain but its exact mechanism remains unclear — what is it?
Methocarbamol: Medication for musculoskeletal pain. It may be used together with rest, physical therapy, and pain medication.
Following the S phase and ending in cytokinesis, this equational cell division splits replicated chromosomes into two genetically identical daughter nuclei — what is the process called?
Mitosis: Cell division into two identical cells. Mitosis is a part of the cell cycle in eukaryotic cells in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
This semiaquatic rodent swims using webbed hind feet while its scaly, flattened tail works mainly as a rudder for steering — what is it?
Muskrat: Species of rodent. The muskrat or common muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent.
Popularized by neurologist George Beard in the 1860s, this diagnosis described fatigue, anxiety, and heart palpitations often blamed on the stresses of modern life — what was the condition called?
Grown worldwide as ornamentals in ponds and known to gardeners simply as water lilies, this widespread genus of aquatic plants also includes species considered weeds — which genus?
Nymphaea: Genus of aquatic plants. Nymphaea is a genus of hardy and tender aquatic plants in the family Nymphaeaceae.
This surgical medical subspecialty treats the ear, nose, and throat — organs connected via the Eustachian tube — earning its specialists the nickname 'ENT surgeons.' What field is it?
Otorhinolaryngology: Medical specialty of the head and neck.

He joined the British Astronomical Association at age 11, compiled the Caldwell catalogue, and hosted the BBC's "The Sky at Night" — the longest-running TV series with its original presenter. Who was this English amateur astronomer?
Patrick Moore: English astronomer, broadcaster and writer (1923–2012)
Structurally related to a calming brain chemical and acting like baclofen or GHB on the same receptor, this anxiety medication can also give a mild dopamine-driven lift at low doses — what is it?

Often at its worst with the very first steps of the day, this common foot disorder inflames the connective tissue supporting the arch and is linked to tight calf muscles and heel spurs — what condition is it?

Plantar fasciitis: Connective tissue disorder of the heel. Plantar fasciitis or plantar heel pain is a disorder of the plantar fascia, which is the connective tissue that supports the arch of the foot.
Sold under the brand name Lyrica, this anticonvulsant amino-acid drug also treats fibromyalgia, nerve pain, and anxiety — which medication is it?
Pregabalin: Anticonvulsant medication. Its use in epilepsy is as an add-on therapy for partial seizures.
Named by the medieval scholar Gerard of Cremona, this black-looking opening in the eye's iris is round in humans but a vertical slit in cats and a horizontal bar in goats — what is it?
Pupil: Part of an eye. The pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Native to western Europe and known scientifically as Ribes rubrum, which widely cultivated berry has escaped into the wild across many regions?
Redcurrant: Flowering plant species in the family Grossulariaceae.
Originating in ancient Rome and used across Europe well into the Late Middle Ages, this numeral system works on which principle?

Roman numerals are a numeral system that originated in ancient Rome and remained the usual way of writing numbers throughout Europe well into the Late Middle Ages. Like many other ancient numeral systems, they are based on the additive principle.
A pharmaceutical chemist with a Dartmouth Ph.D. by day, this American has chaired Anthrocon — one of the world's largest furry conventions — since 1999. Who is he?
Samuel Conway: American chemist and furry fandom personality.
Native to the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada, this endangered conifer is the largest tree species on Earth, with a record height of 94.8 meters — what is it?
Sequoiadendron giganteum: Species of tree native to North America.
Lose your coiled shell entirely and you're called a slug; keep one big enough to retract into and you're this shelled gastropod instead — what creature?
Snail: Shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs.
With eight arms plus two extra tentacles for grabbing prey, this soft-bodied mollusc has an internal chitin rod called a gladius instead of a true skeleton — what creature is it?
Starting his career as a materials engineer and later overseeing the launch of Chrome and Google Drive, who has served as CEO of both Google and its parent company since 2015 and 2019 respectively?
Sundar Pichai: CEO of Alphabet Inc. and Google (born 1972)
Feigning injury or authority to lure victims to his car, this American serial killer murdered young women across five states in the mid-1970s before revisiting their graves. Who was he?
Native to the Mediterranean and containing roughly 350 aromatic species, this herb genus lends its name to a common seasoning found in kitchens worldwide — which genus?
This condition involves a long-term urge to pull out one's own hair, most often from the scalp or around the eyes, and is more common among those with OCD — what is it?
Formed by the fusion of membrane vesicles, this shapeless organelle in plant and fungal cells is basically a water-filled storage sac that can even hold engulfed solids. What is it?
Vacuole: Membrane-bound organelle in cells containing fluid.
Descended from a wild bovine ancestor, this large domesticated animal from the Indian subcontinent now also grazes fields in Italy, the Balkans, and Australia — what is it?
Water buffalo: Species of large bovine. The wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee) is most probably the ancestor of the domestic water buffalo.
Based on how long Earth takes to orbit the Sun, this unit of time comes in tropical and sidereal forms differing by about 20 minutes, with leap years keeping our calendar in sync — what unit?

Year: Unit of time based on Earth's orbit. In scientific use, the tropical year (approximately 365 solar days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, 45 seconds) and the sidereal year (about 20 minutes longer) are more exact.
The symbol for molybdenum is Mo. Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
What is the chemical symbol for nickel?
The symbol for nickel is Ni. Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.

In what year was Ron Howard born?
Ron Howard: Ronald William Howard (born March 1, 1954) is an American filmmaker and actor.
In what year was Jason Sudeikis born?
Jason Sudeikis: Daniel Jason Sudeikis ( suu-DAY-kiss; born September 18, 1975) is an American actor, comedian, screenwriter, and producer.
In what year was Colin Farrell born?
Colin Farrell: Colin James Farrell (born 31 May 1976) is an Irish actor.
In what year was Darren Aronofsky born?
Darren Aronofsky (born February 12, 1969) is an American filmmaker.
In what year was Elizabeth Banks born?
Elizabeth Banks (born Elizabeth Mitchell; February 10, 1974) is an American actress and filmmaker.
In what year was Steve Harvey born?
Steve Harvey: Broderick Stephen Harvey (born January 17, 1957) is an American comedian, radio and television host, actor, writer, and producer.
In what year was Sacha Baron Cohen born?
Sacha Baron Cohen: Sacha Noam Baron Cohen ( SASH-ə; born 13 October 1971) is an English actor and comedian.
In what year was Brian Cox born?
